title: The Strenuous Life
subtitle: Vigor as a Way of Life
intro: Doctors told his parents he might not live to grow up. He built himself a body in a home gymnasium and spent the next fifty years testing it — boxing, wrestling, riding, walking through obstacles rather than round them. Fifteen questions on a creed he practised long before he preached it.
heroAlt: Theodore Roosevelt mounted on horseback in ranch clothes
heroCredit: Theodore Roosevelt in ranch costume. Photograph by T. W. Ingersoll. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What condition made Roosevelt's childhood a physical struggle?
questions.explanation: Asthma, severe enough that his father would drive him through the night in a carriage so the rush of air would help him breathe. Nineteenth-century medicine had almost nothing else to offer.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt as a small boy
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, about two years old. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did his father tell him to do about it?
questions.explanation: Theodore Sr. told him he had the mind but not the body, and that without the body the mind would not carry him as far as it should. "You must make your body." A gymnasium was fitted out on the second-floor piazza and the boy went to work.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt as a young boy
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, about two years old. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

link.label: The man who shaped a president

questions.prompt: Roosevelt's famous 1899 speech gave the creed its name. What was it called?
questions.explanation: "The Strenuous Life," delivered in Chicago in April 1899 while he was governor of New York. Its argument was that a life of ease is not worth living, for a man or for a nation.
questions.credit: "A young head on old shoulders." Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

options: A method of driving game toward guns
Going in a straight line to a chosen point
A timed race between two landmarks
A walking tour of the Washington monuments
questions.explanation: You picked a point and went to it in a straight line, over or through every obstacle and never around. Haystacks were climbed, streams waded, cliffs scaled. Guests were invited along and frequently regretted it. The French ambassador Jules Jusserand kept up, which made his reputation in Washington — and the version everyone tells has him swimming Rock Creek with his gloves still on, in case the party met ladies.
questions.imageAlt: Ted, Archie and Ethel Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill
questions.credit: Ted, Archie, and Ethel Roosevelt one windy day at Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did the press call the group of friends who exercised and rode with President Roosevelt?
questions.explanation: The Tennis Cabinet — an informal circle of officials, diplomats and friends who played tennis, rode, boxed and went on the point-to-point walks. Membership mattered in Washington precisely because it was unofficial.
questions.imageAlt: President Roosevelt and his Tennis Cabinet
questions.credit: President Roosevelt and his Tennis Cabinet. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What happened to Roosevelt's left eye while he was president?
options: He was blinded in it while boxing
A splinter injured it in Cuba
He lost it in a riding accident
questions.explanation: A blow during a sparring session detached the retina and he lost the sight of that eye. He kept it quiet for years — it emerged publicly only later — and gave up boxing for jiu-jitsu. The sources disagree about the year, so the honest thing is to place it in the presidency and leave the date alone. He went on riding, shooting and swimming with one working eye for the rest of his life.
questions.imageAlt: President Roosevelt with his Tennis Cabinet
questions.credit: President Roosevelt and his Tennis Cabinet. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Which martial art did Roosevelt take up in the White House?
questions.explanation: He trained in Japanese jiu-jitsu with an instructor several times a week, on a mat laid down in the White House, and enjoyed being thrown by men half his size. It was unusual enough in 1904 to be newsworthy.
questions.imageAlt: President Roosevelt and his Tennis Cabinet
questions.credit: President Roosevelt and his Tennis Cabinet. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much did Roosevelt's physique change during his Badlands years?
options: He lost weight and never regained it
His weight barely changed at all
He put on fifty pounds or more
questions.explanation: He arrived in 1883 at roughly 135 pounds and left in 1886 at about 170, and it was mostly muscle, put on by roundup work and long days in the saddle. A reporter noted that the voice which had piped “Mistah Speakah” in Albany was now strong enough to drive oxen. The eastern press had to reintroduce him when he came back.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt standing beside his horse on the round-up, 1885
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt on the round-up, 1885. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What became of Roosevelt's asthma after the Badlands?
options: It gave way to chronic heart trouble
It worsened with the cold winters
questions.explanation: It never troubled him seriously again. Whether the cause was the climate, the exertion, or simply growing out of it, the disease that had defined his childhood was gone from his adult life as a serious affliction. It is worth saying that nobody has ever proved the Badlands did it — plenty of asthmatic children in the nineteenth century simply stopped being asthmatic — but he believed the West had cured him, and he acted on that belief for the next thirty years.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt in 1885. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: In 1908 Roosevelt set a fitness standard for army officers and then did what?
options: Exempted himself and the general staff
Applied it only to new recruits
Rode ninety-eight miles in a day
questions.explanation: Officers complained that a required ninety-mile ride over three days was excessive. Roosevelt, then forty-nine, rode from Washington to Warrenton, Virginia and back in a single day — ninety-eight miles, most of the return leg in freezing rain, finishing after dark — and the complaints stopped. He had made the point he wanted to make, which was that he would not ask of the army anything he was not prepared to do himself.
questions.imageAlt: President Roosevelt in the doorway of a ranch house with a dog in his lap
questions.credit: President in doorway of West Divide Creek ranch house. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. One frame of a stereograph card; publisher's mount and caption strip removed.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt do about the brutality crisis in college football in 1905?
options: Called for the sport to be banned outright
Called the colleges to the White House
Set up a federal commission on the game
Left it to the colleges to settle
questions.explanation: Deaths and serious injuries had prompted calls to abolish the game. Roosevelt, who thought rough sport was good for young men but that maiming them was not, brought Harvard, Yale and Princeton to the White House and pressed for reform. The changes that followed led to the forward pass and the body that became the NCAA. He had no jurisdiction over college football whatever; he simply invited people to a room and made it awkward to leave without agreeing.
questions.imageAlt: President Roosevelt and his Tennis Cabinet
questions.credit: President Roosevelt and his Tennis Cabinet. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt insist the strenuous life was ultimately about?
options: Athletic achievement for its own sake
Effort and duty rather than ignoble ease
questions.explanation: He was explicit that he did not mean mere muscle. The doctrine was about a life of effort, labour and useful risk over one of ignoble ease — and he applied it to nations as readily as to men, which is where much of the criticism of it begins. Read as a private creed it is bracing; read as a foreign policy it did real damage, and both readings are available in the same speech.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, three-quarter length portrait, seated. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: How did Roosevelt's insistence on physical risk touch his own family?
options: Only the two elder sons served
All four sons served, and one was killed
His children refused to take part
It did not; he shielded his children
questions.explanation: Ted Jr., Kermit, Archie and Quentin all served, and their sister Ethel went to Paris as a Red Cross nurse. Archie and Ted were wounded; Quentin was shot down over France at twenty. Roosevelt had preached the doctrine for two decades and did not flinch from it publicly — but those close to him said he never recovered, and he outlived his youngest son by less than six months.
questions.imageAlt: Portrait of Mrs. Roosevelt with Quentin
questions.credit: Mrs. Roosevelt, Quentin. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What condition was Roosevelt in physically after the 1913–14 Brazilian expedition?
options: He recovered fully within a few months
Fitter than when he set out
Badly weakened by infection and fever
questions.explanation: A gashed leg turned septic and malarial fever followed. He came out perhaps fifty pounds lighter and never regained his old vigour; the fever came back at intervals for the rest of his life. The strenuous life had a bill, and this was part of it. He was fifty-five, and he had four more years to live.
questions.credit: Putting the tape on the rhino's horn. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How old was Roosevelt when he died?
questions.explanation: Sixty, in his sleep at Sagamore Hill in January 1919, of a coronary embolism. Vice President Marshall remarked that death had to take him sleeping, because awake there would have been a fight.
questions.credit: The Parlor, Sagamore Hill. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.
